content: Ertuğrul or Ertuğrul Gazi (Ottoman Turkish: ارطغرل‎, romanized: Erṭoġrıl, died c. 1280[5]) was the father of Osman I.[6] Little is known about Ertuğrul's life. According to Ottoman tradition, he was the son of Suleyman Shah, the leader of the Kayı tribe (a claim which has come under criticism from many historians[nb 1]) of the Oghuz Turks, who fled from western Central Asia to Anatolia to escape the Mongol conquests, but he may instead have been the son of Gündüz Alp.[3][8] According to this legend, after the death of his father, Ertuğrul and his followers entered the service of the Sultanate of Rum, for which he was rewarded with dominion over the town of Söğüt on the frontier with the Byzantine Empire.[5] This set off the chain of events that would ultimately lead to the founding of the Ottoman Empire.

content:
In 2019 I spent 4 days in a remote village in the Moroccan Rif mountains, without any connection to the Internet. The place was a destiny for pilgrimage because their waters were believed to be miraculous. However, they actually just carried iron; people believed that vomiting would make them purify their bodies, but it actually has bad consequences for health.

Anyway, what was worse about it was how remote the place was, near the Sahara borders, and the whole aura of superstition. I felt like I travelled back to many centuries ago. The place was dirty as hell, we went to the countryside to escape from it but it was plagued by poops because people went there to poop. The waters were extremely dirty of people bathing there and throwing rubbish, and the thought that there was no escape to civilization from there. It was a very bad time, one of the worst in my life with my Covid experience

Most disgusting thing... Hm, I can't decide, so I'll choose two.

1. When I was 12 and bloody stupid, and my scout troop none the better considering what I'm about to say next, we used to have a game we called Pinecone War during our weekly meeting. It was exactly that - we split into teams and threw pinecones at each other. I was dumb and threw anything, including a Red Bull can that was peed into. The guy I marked for death and myself didn't smell very good on our rides home. We also found a better game to play, but that's a story for another time.

2. When I was 19 and bloody tired at work one day, about at midnight on a late shift with one of my usual second closers at Subway, someone came into our store that apparently really needed to use the phone - their ride had left them, and they needed to get home. After waiting for a while, she eventually used the bathroom, and kinda ran out of the store after that. My second looked into the bathroom and realized she had pooped on the floor, "gotten schwifty" if you will. I tied a spare uniform shirt we had over my nose and, after my second had flushed most of the....material, I went to town on that single spot in the bathroom cleaning it. The trash didn't smell good that day, and my paycheck wasn't any better - but that's a given.

Hm. I'll put two again.

1. Leaving home to go to my first apartment near uni. I had relatively little, basically whatever fit in my car (both sets of clothes - a large but obviously, in hindsight, insufficient set of guy clothes I took with me for show, and all the feminine clothes I had stowed away in one of the boxes :trans:, some kitchen stuff, some computer parts and essentials, though I didn't have a desk for the desktop yet). The moment quickly fizzled into a financial situation that, luckily, resolved nicely.

2. My first bar crawl, after the end of my second semester at uni. It's quite a story, and I love to tell it. tl;dr is it was amazing being the only sober one amidst a bunch of happy drunks. My roommate got hammered and was so hyped up about everyone, my classmate basically couldn't stand anymore but was dedicated to die trying, his roommate was all happy emotional about everyone being his friend, and everyone else loved the dress I was wearing. It also made for a fantastic story to tell when my roommate broke his 5th metatarsal (foot bone) on the crawl, and had to attend his wedding with a fancy cane (luckily it fit in with their theme).

content:
I'm loving the answers here, both the meme and the serious ones, and I'd like now to post a text wall about my best moments in life that I hope is inspirational.

Let's start from the beginning. As some of you might know, I'm Asperger's. That pack includes many advantages, but also many disadvantages, difficult to deal with. I was born as a totally unsociable baby, immersed in his own world and who didn't even speak until he was 4. Even with barely speaking by then, I was fascinated by the Encarta virtual tours around historical sites, and very specifically Athens, Rome, Persepolis or Abu Simbel. My parents didn't still have Internet and I got completely teleported to those sites in long afternoons just exploring and learning while having fun. Additionally, when I grew up a bit more, I was absorbed by the strategy game Age of Mythology, which I still play from time to time and who helped me discover many of the myths and heroes from the Greek, Egyptian and Norse mythologies.

My tastes and my way of being were definitely different to the "average" Spanish child of the 2000s, and that brought 9 years of daily bullying in school. My refuge was all the "nerd" things I loved, to which added my other big passion together with Ancient Times: Tolkien. I watched the Lord of the Rings for the first time at the age of 9, and I have never stopped loving it ever since.
author: sammyqahwia

content: My passions were harmless, the people around me were lovely, but why was a whole school bullying me for what I was, for loving what I loved, for trying to be nice and just getting, manipulated, discriminated and isolated from the "cool people"? I didn't understand why people was like that. But it all changed when I left school. I found a highschool that accepted me, teachers that defended me and I made good friends that last until today. I consider the best moment I've ever experienced is my highschool graduation in 2017, when I pronounced a similar speech to this that all the people I loved, family and friends, witnessed, and brought emotions to them. I had there a lot of people that loved me just for how I was, to whose emotions I called, and some answered with tears of joy.
author: sammyqahwia

content:
At the end of highschool, I discovered that there was the possibility to study and get professional in what I always loved: a degree that combined Archaeology, Ancient History and Ancient Philology. I was a bit scared of a new area I was joining and how my experience there could be. However, once again, I've made really good friends there, among those even some professors, I've reached positions such as president of my degree's students association or founding member of my faculty's Student Council. With my association we've collaborated with the major Classical Studies organization in Spain, and we're on the way to collaborate with a well-known videogames company.

After 4 years, I've ended the degree with a work about Ancient Greece in Tolkien's books. I have unified all my passions and made them my profession, earning right today a 9.3/10 as my definitive average mark. I know many of you are now starting uni/college or currently on it: whatever you're studying, whatever is your passion or profession, follow it. Fight, fight, and fight once again. Defeats are hard to deal with, but every victory you earn is a treasure on which you have to lean to continue this constant adventure life is. Those victories, those best moments, are what will inspire you every day to earn more of them. Enjoy every single moment you can and fight to enjoy even more. Only be who you are, you are perfect that way, and don't improve to be better than anyone, but to enjoy more this brief moment of existence.
author: sammyqahwia

content: I hope this little summary inspires anyone around here to be sure of themselves, and I apologize for such a long text. It's a special day, definitely one of my best moments ever, and I want to share it with my fellow TEPers

content:
TEP has always been important since I got integrated in the community, as a window to the outer world. It has always fascinated me how diverse and fun it is, and most of my English knowledge comes from my time here. That knowledge has been really useful for my studies, reaching the point of not reading a single article in Spanish for some of my uni works, and also when travelling to other countries.

My original community under TEP is the Forum RP one: one of its main characteristics is voice chatting every day or two days, where we talk both about IC and OOC stuff. With time, we've ended being really friends of each other and we 80% talk about OOC stuff XD. When the lockdown arrived in March 2020 we were literally all the day VCing, and that was my salvation for the whole month I suffered from Covid: I couldn't move from my bed for three-four weeks, and I spent that time reading Brandon Sanderson and VCing. VCs didn't only help me to go through Covid, but to overcome the depression I had during that month and until August-September.
author: sammyqahwia

content:
Being a whole month at bed helps you to think about *everything*. I always had big doubts about my sexuality, and didn't really want to define myself as X or Y; when I did, I did as straight just to avoid troubles or being badly viewed. However, TEP has several bisexual people that talked about the concept and it sounded familiar. I just thought that it was time to take the step out of the closet. Seeing them so openly talking about it encouraged me to speak to my uni bestie, who is also bisexual, and she explained me fully how it works, so thanks to the encouragement of TEP's LGBT+ friendly stances, I discovered my own sexuality.

The final important change in my life has happened after the creation of my wiki on the Cukish language, the conlang I've been developing for some time. I spoke about it and about TEP in general to my Indo-European prof, and she got so impressed that she offered me a position in her investigation group. At the end I've ended in another different investigation, but that was a really impressive moment and gave a great value to my work here

content:
Started drinking less. Always had a bit of a love/hate relationship with alcohol due to reasons I won't disclose right now. NS helps me keep it in check, limit the drinking; when I got problems, I go bullshit around for a bit, work for the government, check up on WA or such instead of opening another bottle and it works pretty well.

It also, however, reinforced the reality of social bubbles. People tend to keep company with other people of their ilk, and only very few break those bubbles and discover new people with new opinions. Those are fun, tho.

The last but important, I'd mention it allows me to help other people discover themselves and be happier. I'm 26, I've lived through some stuff, I graduated, I worked many jobs for many clients. On NS, you mostly get younger folk, people still not sure how EVERYTHING works, themselves, the world around them, politics, friendships, relationships. I feel like I can help steer them towards discovering it for themselves. Not telling them what to do - that never works and is counterproductive, trust me on that - but gently helping them discover who they are IRL. And, most importantly, ensuring we have a safe, friendly, passionate community that will always support them and never judge them for who they are. I do enjoy that part very much; helps me feel I'm doing something nice for other people.

content:
Alright, I figured it out. I learned to be confident from NS.

When I first started playing NS, I was a hyperactive kid. Then, by 2013, I was suddenly in a leadership position over my region of hundreds. In the face of that, I shaped up. I met my crew, learned what they were good at, and made some friends for that. When I needed stuff done that I couldn't do alone, or shouldn't do alone, I asked my team.

When I returned to NS after a year break for school stuff, I was near my breaking point with my identity, and came out to my region. In doing so, I embraced being myself, shared my story with others, and heard many more since then within the region.

Vandoosa, Libertanny, Zuk, Enlais, Boro, Cinema, and several others I met around with other regions also taught me one common thing: the boss can be just as fun, just as outgoing, and just as much of a meme as the rest of the team. Throughout my years, especially with the scouts, I had learned Leadership in Service, but NS taught me the true placement of brotherhood and love for one another in the leadership scheme.

```A sky darkened
Sighs of boredom
Pressed under the souls
Apathetic mind

Reducted ego
A little whisper
And no one seem to understand
How magnetic those voices are

Like puppets people dance
A voice to command
A voice to be commanded
Every bird sings its song

The sun sets and rises
The rain falls and stops
The clouds passes and goes
Men continue to do their doings

Why does the dog want to feed the cat
Why does the cat want to feed the dog
When the cat doesn't like the dog's food
And the dog, the cat's

Boredom over boredom
Nothing matters anymore
Even the sleep is asleep
As the consciousness drifts

Nobody seems to be there
On the realms of darkness
The moon shines peacefully
The lords couldn't care less

The puppet withers and shivers
The strings, broken
Unable to dance with the others
Nor to paint them
A singular pity```

Card games, more specifically, Cardfight Vanguard.

content:
This isn’t really in any particular order, but it vaguely resembles a Top Five countdown. Here:

AC Origins because that story is one of my favorite things like ever.

Middle Earth Shadow of War without a doubt. LOVED the story with Talion’s downfall and the whole Celebrimbor/Talion fusion thing we had going on. LOVED the gameplay with the nemesis missions and the commanding of your own army and the dominate mechanic. Dialogue was sometimes inorganic and choppy and the graphics were meh but it was worth it.

Fallout 4 was oh so good. I especially loved Far Harbor and Nuka World. Chef’s kiss.

Oh god I loved God of War IV. It was so damn good. The mythology, the gameplay (I cannot TELL you how much I LOVED throwing that axe and calling it back to me it NEVER gets old), the story, everything. The fights were somewhat challenging, but just to the right degree. Except the Valkyries, they’re a nightmare. Anyway I loved it both times I played it.

And of course, last but not least, THE ELDER SCROLLS V SKYRIM WILL ALWAYS OWN MY HEART NO MATTER WHAT.

Honorable mentions:

I liked Destiny 2’s original story a LOT, with the Cabal guy trying to steal the Traveler’s Light. It was very interesting and fun.

I enjoyed For Honor, too, but that was mainly because I was really good at it and had an awesome time fighting online. Story wasn’t half bad either, but I didn’t get too far.

content:
Serious answer:

As it stands, Albrookian lore - and most of the stories I have in my head in general - are largely just ideas and experiences I've had before. And when I was really young, the stores I learned through games shaped my imagination. A childish mispronunciation and misspelling of Final Fantasy 6's Figaro Castle spawned the City-State of Fargo - a Minecraft town, the first name I entered when I made my NS nation 9 years ago back in June, and the destiny of great pioneers and what-not. And through all of my music tastes, I've never once had a period where I said "you know, I don't want to listen to this song right now".

While there's no lyrics, I just hear my imagination (and of course initial awe at the biggest game I played when I was like 7 of course) every time I listen - Edgar and Sabin's theme, the Figaro Castle theme, FF6 - a very nice remix of it.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oWPY85ENo6M

content:
@Daily Question tough questions time.

You can choose only one.
1) Your child is being grown up to be a very moral and compassionste person, but you have a really distant relationship (aka the child doesnt trust you, not necessarily even likes you).

OR

2) Your child has a perfect relation with you - it trusts you, it is kind to you, it comes with problems to you, it feels like it needs you in their life. But the child is not moral, nor compassionate.

Which one do you choose and why.
author: sirserge

content: Btw the question is inspired with Life is Strange.
author: sirserge

content: 1 without any doubt
author: sammyqahwia

content: Oof, this is very difficult. I would probably go with 1) and hope that my child would eventually understand and value how I raised it.
author: pychto

content: I'd still feel great and be proud, and probably I would look into myself instead because the source of the distance is probably my behaviour and not theirs
author: sammyqahwia

content: I'd feel bad about me, not about them
author: sammyqahwia

content: The way I interpreted it, the source of distance would be that it maybe dislikes the lectures and education, in which case I'm not sure how much you can do better if you ultimately want to raise them that way
author: pychto

content: but thats a very good answer, Sammy
author: pychto

content:
And to say my point of view.

Well.  Whilst it could hurt, that your child doesn't trust you and does not even consider you a close person, if their morality and compassion is on the stake, I am ready to lose that close relationship. 

Afterall, the child will remain with me for what, 13? 14? years until it begins becoming independent (idk about other countries, but that's the age here, when people start becooming independent) and if you choose closeness over compassion and morality, then the world will be left with a bad person for the next 50? 60? 70? years?

So what I mean is. I would be OKay with sacrificing my relation with child, if it meant, that it would grow up to be a decent, compassionate and moral human being. Frankly, I'd even have them hate me, if it meant, that they would be even more moral and compassionate. Because one day, those two things might drive them to make a change in a world, that we are living in. 

And we already have enough of people, who do not care and have no compassion. And that compassion and morality will pay the child off far better, than close relation with me.

author: theconstantofchange

content:
1. "Живее на висока нога" - Live on a tall/high leg. Living extravagantly. 
"(Кога ќе дојде) ножот до коска" - (When the) knife (comes) to the bone. When push comes to shove, when you can't delay something further. 
"Го обрав бостанот" - I have harvested the watermelons. Essentially saying that you've screwed up. 

Couldn't find a perfect pangram, so I've added a few more answers to the first question. Additionally I believe there's a Macedonian to English idiom dictionary by Zoze Murgoski floating around on the internet, if you want to have a look for yourself.

content:
I'd recommend Lynn Conway. Born in 1938 in White Plains, she went to MIT in 1955 at the age of 17 and was one of their top students, but didn't earn her degree due to leaving after a failed transition attempt left her depressed, hopeless, and broke. After working as a technician for several years, she went back to school at Columbia and got her B.S. and her M.S.E.E. by 1963. She was hired by IBM in 1964 to work on the ACS project, an early attempt at a modern supercomputer. I don't know what this next part is, seeing as I'm in the half of trans people who *can't* work a computer, but she developed something called a superscalar system which is "a computer architectural paradigm widely exploited in modern high-performance microprocessors."

After learning about pioneering endocrinologist Harry Benjamin (Not queer himself but perhaps one of the most important people in trans history, give him a lookup - He was Christine Jorgenson's doctor), Conway immediately contacted him and began transitioning. The transition went very well medically speaking, but Conway was separated from her two children in the process, and IBM fired her due to the transition in 1968 - a large part of why ACS failed the following year, putting computing research up to 7 years behind where it could have been. 

However, Conway didn't let the complete upending of her life stop her at all. Pioneering the term "stealth" for post-op trans people, she went on to work at Memorex for a few years, and then at Xerox, where she invented "multiproject wafers." Again, no clue what those are, but wikipedia says they "increased production and decreased costs," so I guess they're used in production? She also coauthored *Introduction to VLSI Systems* in this time, which is apparently a very fundamental work in the field of computing. Again, no clue.

In the early 1980s, Conway left Xerox to join DARPA, where she helped pioneer modern advancements in autonomous weapons systems and intelligent weaponry. Yay! (1/2)
author: styxprincess

content:
In 1985, Conway became a professor and associate dean at University of Michigan, where she worked on "visual communications and control probing for basic system and user-interface concepts as applicable to hybridized internet/broadband-cable communications." Fun? She retired in 1998 as professor emerita.

In 1999, she learned that she would be unintentionally outed by Clemson researcher Mark Smotherman as part of his research into the minds behind the ACS project, so she started coming out to her friends and family after 31 years of living stealth, including her boyfriend of 5 years (now her husband of 20 years, so he took it well, I suppose), as well as starting a blog, where she now posts information about TAHC as well as studies on gender identity. In 2000, her coming out attracted attention from major outlets, blowing her story up nationwide, because journalists.

Ever since then, she's been a major rights activist. Specifically, she fought against the acceptance of Blanchard's Typology by psychiatrists, even helping file suit against J. Michael Bailey who helped develop the theory. In 2013, she and colleague Leandra Vicci lobbied the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), the largest global organization of electrical and computer scientists with over 420,000 members in over 160 countries, to add trans inclusive wording to their Code of Ethics, which also established a precedent for hundreds of similar organizations globally.

Finally, in 2020 - 52 years after firing her - IBM issued a formal apology to Lynn Conway for, y'know, basically ruining her life, and also gave her the IBM Lifetime Achievement Award, the highest honor that IBM has the power to give. I'll leave you with these words from the awarding. TL;DR:

"Lynn's extraordinary technical achievements helped define the modern computing industry. She paved the way for how we design and make computing chips today – and forever changed microelectronics, devices, and people's lives." (2/2)

I wonder if I'd prefer staying in my cave daydreaming for the rest of my life, but I want to work in the R&D domain.
So yeah, I'm facing a wall here, and I have no answers.

Sorry for publicly venting. I hardly can take it anymore and the weekly question poses it.

content:
OK so some of my bookies i liky

**"The Memory Police" by Yoko Ogawa [F]** - This was a nifty book, the premise is that everyday the residents of an island forget what one object is. Would really recommend, its a bit slow at the start but it's pretty interesting overall.

**"The Rage of Dragons" by Evan Winter [F]** - A really great fantasy b ook, not sure why I liked it but was pretty nifty.

**"The Toll" by Neal Shusterman [F]** - This book and the series is in is FIRE, its about a world where a large AI tends to guide the planet to the point where no one has to die, so "Reapers" are speciallized killers who curb the population.

**"Homegoing" by Yaa Gyasi [F] **- This book traces two lineages from a mother in 1800s Africa - one becomes stuck in slavery, the other not. It's a really historical fiction book that crosses generations, altho it can be a tad bit boring sometimes. Actually used this for my college admissions essay because i think it's a pretty powerful book

**“This Is How You Lose the Time War” by Amal El-Mohtar [F]** - A romance novel about two warriors who are on opposite sides of a time-travelling conflict. Really lovely although the end does get a bit confusing, highly recommend.

**“The Space Between Worlds” by Micaiah Johnson [F]**- This is a story about travelling between parallel dimensions, loved it.

**“A Memory Called Empire” by Arkady Martine [F]** - A book about an ambassador from a mining colony serving in a really massive space empire that's heavily into eloquence and literature. It's a really awesome book and honestly had some effect on my NS stuff (re: the quotes i used above, plus i kinda am thinking of an award system based on the epitheth one of the nobility in the book has, tho that system probably will never be used lol)
author: imsotiredofthisapp

content:
**“Meet Me In Another Life” by Catriona Silvey [F]** - A book about two people who keep on meeting each other throughout various lives in the same town. The ending is really interesting, but overall I do like how the book treats the concept of soul mates if you can call it that.

**“Elder Race” by Adrian Tchaikovsky [F]** - A book about a wizard in a tower who gets called upon by a princess in need. Though not really - has a twist that's really neat. Wouldn't say the writing is nessecarily the best, but the entire concept tends to endear you to the characters if you like the plot overall.

**“How High We Go In The Dark” by Sequoia Nagamatsu [F]** - A book about a plague and how humanity reacts to it. Another generations spanning book, although this doesn't nessecarily follow character lineages but you can see characters in past stories referenced in future ones. Really cool. Tends to span centuries rather than every generation like Homegoing does.

**“Ogres” by Adrian Tchaikovsky [F]** - A really innovative book where Ogres rule the land and are basically kings & queens. Although not quite. (cw tho it is quite gorey in parts)

content:
At various times my answers have changed. Mind reading was once my main thing, then Omniscience, but now I think “The ability to immediately know the full and correct answer to any question I ask aloud”. Covers the other two nicely.

Speaking more realistically though, I’d wish that everything I try turns out exactly how I want it to. Try to play piano? I can play any song I want to. Try to publish a story? It reaches my target audience. Etc.

There is also a point to be made for “probability manipulation.” The probability of getting a million dollars is 0? Make it 100. Etc.

However those last two are boring because they try to “win”, which as I’ve implied, I don’t like. So realistic and not boring: I wish to not need to worry about material concerns such as having a house, enough food and water, not being in debt, etc. so that I can focus on doing what I want to do.

content:
*Generally, we’re better at remembering what we’ve seen than what we’ve heard. And some people do have better visual memory than others. Highly Superior Autobiographical Memory (HSAM) is a condition that has been identified in fewer than 100 people worldwide. People with HSAM can recall past events in great detail, along with the exact dates when they occurred. For example, they may be able to tell you what they ate for lunch on May 1, 1999 (and that it was a Saturday).

Their memories are exceptional, but certainly not as perfect as actual photographs. Doctors have yet to understand what exactly is happening in the brains of individuals with HSAM, and tests reveal there is no particular ability that appears to underpin the condition. Results from one study suggest that people with HSAM are no better at acquiring memories – they are not superior learners – but are simply better at retaining memories.*

content:
Last night I took 5 hours in one setting to read Meet Me In Another Life cover to cover. It was really good. I like the ideological conflicts, the way it treats their growing awareness, and the bond they form by the end, which I don’t think can really be defined as anything. The way the ending called back to a lot of the stuff that was talked about earlier and how they worked through the mystery was really cool. By the like third life I fully understood the characters and it wasn’t because they were shallow by any means. There were other little things that I liked too that aren’t really worth mentioning.

Also, the bait and switch at the end was really impactful, and I felt like it was a satisfying conclusion. Definitely one of the best ones I’ve read this year (maybe I’ll make a ranking and talk about the books I read and make it UTEP because the entire point of UTEP is very clearly for me to dump random thoughts and interests)

content: Identity does not change based on states of mind, but it is true that subconscious thoughts, and maybe indeed those of which you might not otherwise speak, would rise to the surface. This includes things you may not always agree with sober, or you may keep suppressed not because it’s wrong but because it is socially disruptive or destructive, such as perhaps admitting attraction to someone whose platonic relationship you may not wish to endanger or revealing a secret which you (or the one whose secret you are supposed to be keeping) consider to be far too personal to be revealed. In this sense, you would not otherwise allow these subconscious thoughts to cause such disruption, and so the cause would clearly be the inebriation, but that does not take the blame from you, not if you indeed chose that state of inebriation. If your inebriation reveals a poor characteristic of yourself, such as exposing discriminatory thoughts, then it is still you who holds those beliefs, and it is you who are at fault for keeping them.

@Daily Question 

Broadly, what genre of video game do you prefer? RPG, First Person Shooter, grand strategy, etc.

More specifically, what aspects, themes, etc. do you like/look for in a game? Do you like having a lot of choices or next to none? Do you like an open world to explore, or a “railroad” to go down? Do you like a game that has a story or not?

author: iowan29

content:
It’d be a toss-up between whether I prefer Action RPGs, JRPGs, or FPS more. But generally if I’m just grabbing a game to have some fun it’s one of those.

Working backwards, I think the story is the most important part a lot of the time. There doesn’t need to be a massive story-dump - it could just be revealed over time or told in another way, say if it is intended to be a co-op or unique experience. But generally some direction instead of just being plopped into a game is neat. It gives something more to talk about when everything’s done and gives a good sense of purpose, and some emotional value from things.

I tend to enjoy there being clear linear paths, *hand wiggle*. It might be better to explain by example - when I’m playing some JRPG or relatively simple game where there’s only one obvious way to go, it’s pretty easy to figure out and do it on my own. But if I get plopped into a situation where there’s 8 valid ordinal directions to go immediately and the main story conveniently takes a break to let me explore, I’m going to ask for help from a guide if I haven’t already. There is such a thing as “too linear” - especially in VNs I notice. But generally I’m happy with a few trail markers, if not always the railroad.

This response is already getting long so I’ll stick to a few aspects. I enjoy cosmetic customization, but mechanical customization can get carried away. I enjoy finding a weapon and being told “This is a Thing. It has these stats. Maybe you can upgrade it later.” instead of “This is a Thing-41413 with 7 pre-set mod pieces and 5 more empty slots, all ready for your fine-tuning.”; likewise when I get a new party member I enjoy being told “This is Bob, or maybe you can name him something else. He’s a black mage. Have fun with him and learning his story!” instead of “This is Steve. He’s another dude maybe with a story you get to fully customize with our expansive job system.”

Games that make me feel and think good.

author: theconstantofchange

content: Why can't we know what happens when we make a measurement of a quantum system?
author: daughteria

content: god i actually have to know this for my degree
author: kyrla_

content: basically there's this thing called a wavefunction (Ψ) and it describes everything you'd need to know about a particular atom or molecule or system or whatever
author: kyrla_

content: and you can get that information out of it by using an operator which is notated by a letter with a hat on top of it but unicode only lets me put it to the side so we'll say A^
author: kyrla_

content: so if you wanted to find out what the B level of Ψ was you'd calculate B^ Ψ and you'd get out some multiple of Ψ (hopefully)
author: kyrla_

content: when B^ Ψ = bΨ (i.e. it is a multiple of Ψ) then you can say that Ψ is an Eigenfunction of B^
author: kyrla_

content: this is how you get the semi-famous equation H^ Ψ = EΨ
author: kyrla_

content: H^ is called the Hamiltonian Operator and when you perform the Hamiltonian Operator on your wavefunction you get out (your wavefunction multiplied by) the energy of the system
author: kyrla_

content: in quantum mechanics you do this to your wavefunctions like all the time
author: kyrla_

content: ok so
author: kyrla_

content: there's another thing called a Commutator and it's a way of comparing operators
author: kyrla_

content: and it takes the form [ A^ , B^ ]
author: kyrla_

content: and it's just equal to A^ B^ - B^ A^ (when all combined like this, this is also an operator)
author: kyrla_

content: so [A^,B^]Ψ = A^ (B^ Ψ) - B^ (A^ Ψ)
author: kyrla_

content: if you've chosen your operators such that the order doesn't matter, then [A^,B^]Ψ = 0 and your operators officially Commute
author: kyrla_

content: because A^ (B^ Ψ) will = B^ (A^ Ψ)
author: kyrla_

content: and if [A^,B^] = 0 then it is possible to find an eigenfunction of A^ that is also an eigenfunction of B^
author: kyrla_

content:
and therefore we can simultaneously and precisely know the values of A^ Ψ and B^ Ψ
(because we can use the same Ψ to achieve A^ Ψ = aΨ *and* B^ Ψ = bΨ)
author: kyrla_

content: a problem arises when we pick the two operators **position** and **momentum**
author: kyrla_

content: the operator for position is x^, and the operator for momentum is px^
author: kyrla_

content: x^ = just multiply by x
author: kyrla_

content: px^ = -iħ ∂/∂x (i.e. take the partial derivative with respect to x (i.e. what is the change in Ψ per unit of x) and then multiply it by -iħ)
author: kyrla_

content: unfortunately, [ x^ , px^ ] Ψ does not equal 0
author: kyrla_

content: when the maths all shakes out it ends up being equal to iħ
author: kyrla_

content: therefore:
author: kyrla_

content: x^ and px^ do not Commute, instead they are Complementary
author: kyrla_

content: and that means it is impossible to **simultaneously** and **precisely** know the position *and* the momentum of a particular thing
author: kyrla_

content: momentum = mass × velocity so you might also hear it as position and velocity, or position and speed
author: kyrla_

content: and that's the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
author: kyrla_

content: you can also use the commutator to find how much uncertainty there actually is
author: kyrla_

content: standard deviation = σ, and one thing that just is true about the universe is that σA multiplied by σB is equal to at least half of the absolute value of the expectation of the Commutator
author: kyrla_

content: and when you chuck  [ x^ , px^ ] Ψ = iħ Ψ into that, it spits out this also semi-famous equation (you may also see the uncertainty written as Δ instead of σ)
author: kyrla_

content:
**TLDR**
- when you make a quantum measurement, that involves throwing an Operator at a Wavefunction that describes the thing you're measuring
- if the result is a constant multiple of your original Wavefunction then that Wavefunction is called an Eigenfunction of the Operator, and your constant multiple is the value of your measurement
- if the Commutator of two Operators equals zero, then your Wavefunction can be an Eigenfunction of both of those Operators at the same time
- which would mean you can make exact measurements at the same time
- the Commutator of Position and Momentum does not equal zero
- therefore you cannot know both simultaneously and precisely the position and momentum of the thing you're measuring

content:
Exactly twelve hours later (plus the 12 or so minutes it took to write an answer I completely deleted and then however long it takes to write this one), I will now answer this in retrospective rather than prospective.

Nothing. Not really. Today was a bad day to ask this because it was what I’d consider somewhat of my day off from the stresses of being a person. Most of today was spent with mindless entertainment, and now a significant (but small) amount has been spent on contemplative self-reflection, some of which is attached to this question.

So I’m going to replace the word “today” with “every day” because that’s a more general thing I can more easily speak to. The question is now “What are you doing every day to make the world a better place?”

And this is an interesting question because it’s one I’ve considered in these past two or three weeks. I’ve decided that, no matter how bad a mood I am in, I will try to do something good every day. This is often super small (some would say negligible) such as holding the door open for someone or something, but can also be pretty big - recently a good thing I did was offer serious advice to someone who was experiencing a problem with burnout, something I actually want to follow up on soonish.

I’d like to specify - it’s not like I’m doing the good to fulfill a quota or anything, I genuinely just do it because I want to do some good, and like that example of something big was something that 100% would have happened anyway. But the mindset is nice to have, because I think of how it encourages the small good things, things so small, so perhaps negligible that you might have just not done it. I think those things are important. Something they say in the Good Place is to make doing good a habit and then work on the motivation, and I think that’s something this does.

There’s more but I’m reaching the character limit and it’s getting deep.

content: How does sapience differ from sentience?
author: y_n0t_

content: (For clarification, more than anything)
author: y_n0t_

content:
I’ve heard it said as the difference between intelligence and wisdom, as in an animal can be aware of it’s surroundings and connect this knowledge to previous experience and biological impulses to come up with clever or creative reactions, but doesn’t actually realize that that is what it was doing. There is no complex thought involved, just instinct and basic thought. Another thing I’ve heard is sentience is individuality but sapience is recognizing individuality, but that doesn’t really make sense, I don’t think.

Wikipedia calls it “transcendent wisdom” or “ultimate reality”, an idea of objective and subjective truth that defines judgement, understanding, and compassion. I think this is closer to my preconceived notions of sapience.

It’s difficult to define the borders of this thing because it’s difficult to know and understand, we just don’t have enough information to make that kind of judgement. Additionally there’s a level of subjectivity. When someone says “X are people, too” they are usually implying sapience of a sort, I think, and the advanced intelligence of animals like crows and dolphins and octupi are suspiciously close to some definitions of sapience, written or un. Defining sapience completely kinda removes some of its value as a label, I think. You can’t really do it empirically, a lot of it is really abstract.

It’s why if we ever find other sapient species out there, we will have this discussion as a greater society and culture and many will try to use that opportunity to change what sapience is in order to fuel their own bigotry, something represented by Sci Fi xenophobia.

content:
For a project in school, I had to create my own country. Based partially in my original idea for Aivintis I constructed my utopia with dominant cultural values of justice, cooperation, progress, democracy, authenticity, and forethought.

Perhaps the strangest of these at a glance, I will be talking about authenticity for the purposes of this question. If anyone else wants to use any of those six ideals as the basis of their answer to the question, be my guest.

I defined the cultural value of authenticity as being true to oneself, maintaining a complex individual identity, and not compromising one’s values. An authentic life, as I interpret it, is being yourself. Not censoring your opinion, not backing down from those who wish to prevent you from being you, being honest in conversation and in your actions (not going against your word, not saying things you don’t believe, not cheating anyone, or betraying anyone’s trust).

I chose this value for the project because I felt like it was important to my life. 

Something I truly struggle with is speaking up against injustice in everyday life. I am ashamed to say that I have stayed silent in the face of transphobic rhetoric, for example, and I believe that to be one of my biggest flaws in need of correcting. I try to speak up when I’m uncomfortable or when I feel like someone I know is causing harm. 

I try to answer questions like the one I am answering now, those deep questions that people sometimes ask you, half-expecting a half-baked answer, but I do it to the best of my ability. One time, someone asked me if I thought nihilism was inherently pessimistic, one of the most randomly timed questions I’ve ever been asked, and I spoke my mind about the subject. I try to be honest about how I wanna live my life, and how I see life and the universe as a whole.

I try not to lie. Perhaps this ideal is better defined as truth rather than authenticity. But I try not to lie and I do feel bad when I do. (1/?)
author: theconstantofchange

content:
I try to tell the truth when asked, and I try to seek truth in matters greater than myself. I subscribe to unbiased news sources. I watch educational videos on YouTube. I try to strip away bias to reach a level of critical thinking which I would define as authentic.

I try to be authentic in my writings. Sometimes, other media inspires me to write something, but I don’t think that’s a bad thing. I feel authentic when I look at the way some book or movie told a story, ache for the opportunity to tell the same story, and realize that I would not be able to bring something new to it. I seek to write only things I can bring my own voice to, my own mind. I think that is authentic to my values and my work. 

I keep secrets. Perhaps this is why authenticity isn’t truth. I am true to myself and to my loved ones, even if that means not spreading objective truth. Or at least I try to be. It’s difficult sometimes.

I think my individual identity is complex and unique. Authentic, in that way. So many wildly different things have shaped me. The media I consume forms a strange pattern I think, when urban fantasy horror podcasts and fantasy shows made for kids both contribute much to the questions I ask myself and the way I act towards others. I have friends of many different races, sexualities, genders, and of many different lives. I like to think that diversifying my perspective allows it to evolve on its own, and I like to think that makes it authentic in a way. (2/?)
author: theconstantofchange

content:
One of the things I kept in mind when defining authenticity as a cultural value was the idea of trans people transitioning and gay people living openly without fear. To conform to authenticity, then, I figured, would be to be out and unapologetically yourself. In my imaginary utopia it was as easy done as said, but in real life, factors sometimes prevent people from living authentically to their gender identity or sexuality. Hate holds them back, or fear of hate. Many of my friends just kinda assume I’m queer, which I assure them doesn’t bother me, but it’s kinda a running joke that I just won’t tell them. I haven’t come out to anyone IRL. I’m scared, in many ways. And I guess it means I’m straying from the ideal of authenticity. Not in a way many people would fault me for, but I wish I could summon the courage to tell someone. Even just one close friend.

I keep my promises. This is easy, it goes hand in hand with not lying. Not as in east to do, because it can be hard, but as in easy to address. It’s not a complicated topic in and of itself. I keep my word as best I can.

Cheating is more complex, I feel, or at least academically. Because personally, I find nothing morally wrong with cheating on a test, but I do have a problem with plagiarism. While I might google an answer for an online test with no one watching, I don’t think I’ll ever steal an essay from someone, or even a part of one. I refuse to pass off ideas that weren’t my own as my own, because one of my deepest desires is to have really truly good ideas. To think for myself and to have thoughts that people find interesting or particularly helpful. This is authenticity, I think.

Cheating in the sense of prospering off of another’s misfortune, however, is another easy one. It’s not hard to not take advantage of people, I feel, and so I feel like I do good in this category.

(3/4)
author: theconstantofchange

content: I like to think I am true to myself. I like to think that I live authentically, that I don’t struggle in being myself. And indeed one could point towards a lot of evidence for that. I make weird jokes that no one gets sometimes, I say things people disagree with, and despite sometimes feeling like it’s not appreciated, I speak my mind. I have my own behavioral quirks that other people notice, which I think is a tell-tale sign of someone being themselves. I live by my ideals. Which is kinda what this whole question is about. But even aside from authenticity, I try to live by other ideals, such as the ones I mentioned. I try to be fair in my judgment. I try to be kind in my actions. Etc. But I am human and thus I am flawed. So I have my own shortcomings. I have parts of myself that I’m afraid to show to people. I am afraid to be myself around strangers, certainly, but even around some of my closest friends, I keep secrets about my own identity, or my own thoughts, or my own desires. Sometimes, as a joke, I say my spine is one of those toothpick and marshmallow towers, and while I think that’s quite the dramatization, I say it because I feel like I am fundamentally prone to cowardice. When I feel judged or pressured, I think it’s easy for me to fold. To fall silent in the face of injustice. To keep the secret of who I am to myself. To not share my pain, lest it become a burden to others. In falling victim to these flaws, I am not living according to that ideal of authenticity. I mean I suppose authenticity includes acknowledging your mistakes and working past them. Still, though, I don’t wanna give myself an A for effort because I want to keep working at it. I know I can’t be perfect, but I can be better. So it’s an ongoing process, I think. I think it’s like that with living according to any ideal. Or just living in general. But yeah. (4/4)
author: theconstantofchange

content: The knot in my flag represents four ideals: Unity, empathy, equality, and depth. I am going to focus on depth because it is the most likely to be misunderstood. In my view, depth is the antonym of superficiality. Going beyond the first glance and listening to the emotions and reasons that motivate is a way to gain depth. Having the capacity to consider multiple points of view even when you disagree with the original position is valuable. But depth alone is inadequate: One possible issue with this ideal is that it can lead to over-complicated policies. Depth is part of what differentiates intelligence from wisdom. In the problem solving process, you can have a complete solution without much depth in favor of simplicity.

There's also a difference between *asking* deep questions and *being* deep. Many people know me for one thing or another, either art or code or languages or rock climbing, but not all at once. At work, I often feel restricted by the specification.

author: theconstantofchange

content: Mine is "For small creatures such as we the vastness is bearable only through love." This is a Carl Sagan quote that I simply adore. Something core to my personal philosophy is an outright, violent rejection of nihilism, and this reflects that well. I know, logically, that we are so small in this vast universe - I've drawn on it for horror. But I refuse to accept that it means we don't matter, because I choose to believe that we make our own meaning for the universe, because we make our own meaning for our own little universes, universes made up of the coffee shops, bookstores, classrooms, and bedrooms we haunt. I also believe the meaning of life is love - be it romantic, platonic, familial, or directed at pets, nature, your special interests, or the world as a whole. Love is how you make meaning, love is meaning, and love is the only way to make it through the horrible reality of our lives, from the conflict and abuses all around us to the very simple smallness of our world.

content: (1/11) Expensive. All the pros and cons that come with the word. I spent every dollar I made last year and I think more. Out of it I got at least the following, which I'll break up into singular hecking posts because I cannot for the life of me be succinct in post count with automod.

content: (2/11) I got to see what a hospital in Vegas was like and how rough using crutches is if you never got hurt, and thus had no experience with them, before. Luckily I didn't need them late the next day, and the numbers I was dreading in my head were way worse than the bills actually ended up being. This bill probably sucked the most to anticipate, pay, and now here's hoping I can get the money back from work following a bunch of questions and claims I don't want to do. :pain:

content: (3/11) Speaking of Vegas I got to spend a week there on business. There I ate some good food, saw a show at the fancy new Sphere, and enjoyed the Amazon Web Services conference I was there for. There I learned some cool new network and cybersecurity stuff, and a few sessions on established AI industry standards so my personal hate doesn't seep into my work.
author: aurorayukihime

content: (4/11) I went to see TWO vtuber Hololive concerts. On the same weekend. I elaborated later on, but meh - I gotta rewrite all of this anyway. Speaking of that convention...
author: aurorayukihime

content: (5/11) I enjoyed the New York Times Square area. There I ate some extremely tasty food, saw the Statue of Liberty, went to that convention where I saw the concerts, played some cool games, and bought some cool merch stuff at. Coincidentally I was at that same convention center for another AWS business event earlier in the year. For the meme I stayed at the same hotel.
author: aurorayukihime

content: (6/11) Speaking of the shops at the convention, I continued to expand my weeb merch collection. I grabbed some of my waifu Akai Haato's, or Haachama's, the worldwide strongest idol of Hololive's 1st Generation, stuff as it came out; got some cute figures too; and following what's next on the list I also started dabbling in Suisei's merch - fittingly expensive as the diamond in the rough, so I'm being a bit more selective.
author: aurorayukihime

content: (7/11) I planned and executed "Project D4K", where I coincided the release of Diablo 4 with an Xbox and TV upgrade for 4K gaming and watching. The Xbox can play CDs and blu-rays now. The Xbox I christened with Suisei's name, and the TV with the ultimate idol Hoshino Ai's name :aiWow: I wanted a "starry, perfect, flashy center idol" theme here after all.
author: aurorayukihime

content: (8/11) I then proceeded to enjoy a week off of work for Diablo 4. I'd only taken maybe the odd long weekend up to this point. It felt good to sign off for a bit.
author: aurorayukihime

content: (9/11) I also had to pay some more serious bills, given all of the above was simply fun or warranted expenses enjoying said fun. :haachamaNotLikeThis_G: I live in the old family house, and my folks don't really care much about the state of it anymore. So I hired for, arranged, and paid in full repair to the original wood siding and vinyl cladding onto the house. Just in time to prevent the insurance policy from being cancelled :catJAM:

content: (10/11) I also helped out my brother who was in some pretty depressing debt during one of my peaks this year.

content:
More JRPG's always good - especially through the Dragon Quest series I'm enjoying slight deviation, uniqueness, and series consistency in the genre, especially appreciating the fourth game having entire chapters focusing on specific characters (paving the way for Octopath, FF6, and a Sailor Moon JRPG for what comes to mind immediately), and expanding the cast to include even capturing enemies in basically proto-Pokemon in the fifth game (which could arguably have paved their way, being _first_ in a massively culturally influential series itself)

Judging from the first game's remake the Atelier series certainly delivers on these points - it's like the first Harvest Moon merged with a JRPG. The days mattering, the looming deadline, but the all familiar grinding, resource management, and crafting... I am eager to see how it all evolves, and evolved (acknowledging I'm playing a remake with QoL)

content:
23 is also one of my favorite numbers. Sammy may have rubbed off on me in that respect, but there's more to it. Technoblade was 23 years old when he died. Furthermore, 20**23** is the year of democracy for Aivintis.

13 is another. I like the occult implications, the lucky or unlucky nature, depending on who you ask, that sort of thing. It is an easy number to incorporate into my horror lore every once in a while. Repeating phrases 13 times, for example, or having 13 members of a group, stuff like that. In Throne of Glass, there are 13 witches to a coven, which just reinforced it for me.

2109 is another number I really like. It may not look like it but it's a multiple of 111. I kept adding 111 to a calculator one year, and when I got to that, I thought it was a cool number in how, although it seemed to have no discernible pattern, it was the continuation of a repetitive string of symmetry.

content:
“I dreamed that God would be forgiving.” I Dreamed a Dream from Les Miserables. This line really stands out from what is a phenomenal song imo because it stands in the face of what the protagonist of Les Mis believes. Jean Val Jean is a very religious character, the very end scene literally depicts him going to heaven to be with all the people who died during the runtime of the musical, and this line draws a stark contrast between the “average person” that Fantine represents and somebody who becomes very privileged, that being Val Jean. Fantine spends the last of her time alive, after being fired from Val Jean’s factory, as a very impoverished person. Val Jean can only believe in a loving, forgiving god, because he stands in a position of wealth/power, whereas Fantine at the very least has serious doubts about whether God exists at all partially because of her former belief that God would be a forgiving being. But clearly, at least to Fantine, God can’t be forgiving, if he’s real, because a forgiving God would not condemn her to the life she has to live at this point in the musical. She admits in this song she’s made mistakes, but what mistakes she has made, she believes, that a forgiving God would forgive her and allow her at least some comfort.

Ironically, that comfort does come at the very end of her life, when Val Jean steps in to tell Fantine that he will take care of her daughter after she dies, and that if he’d known what he knew now he wouldn’t have allowed her to be fired from his factory.

content:
Southern France:
Solemn/sober-Like to speak lots of French but want you to speak French to them first otherwise they won’t reply at all; sometimes smile but don’t seem so keen on strangers/tourists; some older persons can be very rude, sometimes hate you for being German but take your money anyways (if u rent a small place to stay for holidays); can be sometimes nice (definitely not in PACA though)

Northern Italy: 
Culture-loving but serious; will welcome you but also keep the distance, love to share their culture with you; though they also take their culture very seriously (a bit too seriously imho) and can be very nice and pleasant (just don’t do the German thing and talk about politics first time with them); generally speaking, my view might be biased here bc I love the language (i an learning it right now) and culture; Venezia is, despite over-tourism, always worth a visit. Sooo much to see overall in Italy. 

South Tyrol (yes, I am making this its own thing):
Friendly and nice.
Some people from Italy proper can be very stuck up and refuse to speak to you, but if you are German and talk to a South Tyrolian, they will be very nice to you and welcome you with open arms. Offer you food and lodging. At least one of the two. Especially in the countryside, if you meet them and talk about the beautiful valleys-and-mountains-region they live in; generally very friendly (with a few exceptions here and there). Overall a very positive experience, I seriously recommend granting them more autonomy. Also make good food, especially sausages and ham and bacon and everything (up to German standards). 
((never had them myself but if you like potato dumplings et al, I recommend going there in early autumn when they have their dumpling festival))

Catalunya:
Warm, welcoming, good spirited.
Great, warm-hearted, and particularly queer folks, at least a fair bunch of them; almost always very friendly (especially to tourists); like to help out, like to stay friendly and also be gae.

author: stardustfromouterspace_4687

content:
Cyprus:
Culture-loving and good-hearted.
Very friendly, seem to like tourists from other countries a lot, love talking about their culture to you, or just help you partying; very nice and always ready to lend a helping hand; seriously care about their environment (a good bunch of them), very lovely and sweet people. 

The Canaries (Lanzarote):
overall unfriendly 
(my perception may be flawed here, since I only interacted with a few of them, but the few I talked to did not appear very nice).
Will answer all your questions (about a building, person, etc.) but only hesistantly; and though I wasn’t visibly queer back then, they made the impression not to like queer folks (at least to me). Not rude but very distanced and cold people, from the ones I met. 

Dominican Republic:

idk, got a very mixed impression of them.
Some people there are really nice, especially to tourists, they like to celebrate their culture with you, but some others are very cold and distanced; one tourist guide we had seemed nice at first but was constantly joking about Germans and WW2, overall left a bad impression in my mind; second time, the tourist guide was very different, actually keen on talking about his culture and getting to know yours, also showed me Mamajuana (no, not Marijuana, Mamajuana):
You basically buy a bottle filed with certain herbs, then buy red wine or rum (or similar schnapps), then fill that into the herbs mixture and let it rest overnight for a few nights, and *tada* ✨ you got Mamajuana. Folks can very friendly and warm there but also very distanced. The country is very pro-USA, one of the few countries in the world where baseball is taken seriously and the national sport instead of football, and whilst in 2015, USD were solemnly accepted everywhere, this changed 4 years later, and the Euro became far more known there. Also accepted the Euro by then. They seem to not have been a fan of orange Florida man. 
But never drive on your own there, unless you are from the country.

content:
With time I've come to accept my own contradictory nature and way of being. It's a position my life and personal context have put me into, and while many people can be very coherent with all their aspects of their life in a socially accepted way, some people, like myself, simply can't.

That doesn't affect the fact that when I give my word, I really do. My complexity doesn't affect other people, some even love it more than I do myself!! (Some dislike it but I don't care anymore) And they trust me because I want to stay true to myself —the only way to be happy—, now even true to, and open and honest about my own contradictions, so they know the truth in both my good and bad words, and that has led to many people trusting me. A difficult position to be many times, but one I'm thankful about.

content:
My favourite piece of visual art?
Its source has been lost on the wired. It's a drawing of Ib, a red-eyed long-brown-haired anime girl mirrored through a glassy soil with Mary, a blue-eyed long blonde-haired girl with an elegant green dress
It comes from the horror game "Ib" and express the ambivalence of the relationship between those two. The calm, thoughtful, Curious Ib and the desperate, capricious, greedy Mary. I love the reflection in the soil as an effect, and how epurated and clean the picture is.

I can think of another one, but it would spoil a certain anime movie.
It's a story of a man unable to love who raises a girl lost in a forest, and the girl kinda saves the man from his loneliness. There's this scene who gives me goosebumps everytime 😭 

Another piece of visual art? Hmmm...
I'll avoid getting religious...

So... Uhm...
I'll settle with this one. A bit of cheating since it's an ending. It comes from Shadow's house. It's a mansion where faceless people who emits soot lives as aristocrats. They use "living dolls" to do their chores. On the left, you have Emilico, who can transform the darkest dystopias in a theme park. On the right, her mistress, Kate. She's cool and composed. I once again love the symmetry that picture (and to an extent scene) shows. This picture is a way to show what I meant with the first one ✨

content: not everyone with anxious attachment has low self worth or self esteem, however it is a common trait. people with anxious attachment style react to their fear of abandonment by trying to cling onto what they have, being stressed if any events trigger that fear (similar to rejection sensitive dysphoria), need lots of communication and attentiveness. usually as children, their parents/guardians would be very attentive/emotionally available at times, but would be suddenly inconsistent, or even some that rely on their children emotionally. people with avoidant attachment have fear of intimacy, they believe if they allow someone to get too close they will hurt them, in stressful emotional situations they shut down/withdraw. these people’s childhood typically had parents/guardians that were detached and cold, or absent altogether. disorganized attachment style is a combination of the two, fear of intimacy and abandonment. there is a really good site with well explained overviews i will send if i can find

content:
@Daily Question 

Omg we gotta rename it to daily question at some point.

That is one lengthy question but this topic is quite interesting.

Did you guys know there's... several types of empathy?

Which ones do you think you have and how intense are they?

🧠 Cognitive Empathy: Being able to understand / identify another person's emotions on logical level. Without affective empathy you know what other person is feeling (or how to awake specific feeling in them) but you do not feel it on yourself (you consider it more a fact).

❤️ Affective Empathy: Can be defined as emotional resonance. You feel *with* the person. Meaning their emotions are mirrored as your own. It's like identifying other people's emotions using your emotions, not logic.

💓 Somatic Empathy: Now this is kind of connected to the above, except you can share someone's physical pain. This can go anywhere from feeling someone's emotions that are further empowered by physical sensation in your body (changed heart rate, feeling of "weight" below heart and other nervous system sensations) to feeling pain in the place the other person is feeling it.

:hug: Compassionate Empathy: Feeling concerned for someone's state and feeling extremely motivated to help them (release them from that state). 

Pssst.

There is also 🎵 Aesthetic / Artistic Intelligence which is generally different concept from Cognitive Empathy. It involves knowing how people will react to specific sounds (melody, tone of voice, music genre) and / or visual stimuli (colors, brightness, images, videos).
